What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
In these graphs I notice that college programs that are not as prestigious as others have a harder time at making the tournament, no matter how good they play. I also noticed that the points were not as much as the men's bracket.

raw_comment:
What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
I notice that there aren’t that many upsets in the round of 64 of the women’s bracket, I only counted 8 upsets. I notice in both brackets that there is a mix of very well-known universities and some lesser known universities. I also notice that west coast teams did not go as far as east coast teams.

What do you wonder?
I wondered how teams qualified for the tournament and found out that they either won their conference’s tournament or qualified by “having enough talent”. I wonder how the NCAA determines if a team has enough talent. I would want to see a study that goes into the factors of why east coast schools perform better than west coast schools.

How does this relate to you and your community?
Without debate, many people in my community including myself follow college and professional sports. I know people who filled out brackets to predict who would win. There are also people from our community who played in the tournament.

1.I noticed that the ranking is by colleges and that LSU is going against Iowa for the women’s ranking. For the men’s bracket the game is between Connecticut and S.D State. I also noticed that there was a category of the first four in the bottom and there were six teams under that title. There’s also titles of each of the games on the top, it starts with round 64 and the date then works to the final on April 2nd. Lastly, some of the same colleges play for the men’s and women’s bracket. However, if one college for the men’s bracket gets disqualified in the first round, for example Iowa, then that same college can do better in the women’s bracket, for example Iowa in the women’s bracket made it to the finals.

It also relates to me because if basketball is something that interests me I would want to choose the best college for that sport.
4.This graph displays the college basketball event called march madness, it is divided by a men’s bracket and women's bracket.

raw_comment:
I notice that the men’s basketball teams usually scored higher points compared to the women’s side. When looking at the difference between the points that each team scores, I notice that on the men’s side the points are usually pretty close to each other compared to on the women’s side the point difference is usually a little greater. For example, on the left side of the women’s bracket Notre Dame scored 59 points and Maryland scored 76. While on the right side of the men’s bracket T.C.U scored 72 points and Arizona state scored 70 points.

I wonder why Iowa and L.S.U scored higher points compared to S.D state and Connecticut. Throughout the whole bracket you can see that the men’s basketball teams usually always have bigger numbers compared to the women’s side.

This relates to me and my community because in the bay area basketball is an extremely popular sport and it's also very important to my family. Knowing how to analyze points and understanding the basketball brackets helps me better understand the whole concept of basketball.

raw_comment:
What do you notice? Looking at the bracket, I noticed that the number 1 seed teams for both the men and women were defeated in the early rounds of the NCAA Basketball Tournament. I also noticed that, surprisingly, the scores in the championship game for the women’s tournament was significantly higher than the score from the men’s side. I find this interesting because usually, the men in the NCAA are the ones who score more points. 
What do you wonder? I never really watch College Basketball, so I wonder if Divisions play a role in the college basketball ranking system. Do all the teams in the bracket come from different divisions? Or is the entire bracket revolved around a single division?
How does this relate to you and your company? This relates to my community because my school revolves around sports. Whenever I would arrive on campus, I would hear a lot of my friends and other students talk about sports, whether it would be about basketball, football, soccer, etc. Since the NBA playoffs just started, we get to gauge and compare the similarities and differences between an NBA bracket and a college bracket. 
What’s going on in this graph? This graph explicitly shows the progress of college basketball teams as they make their way through the tournament. The graph includes the name of all college teams, including their team record, seed placing, and game scores involving themselves and the team they went against. Title = “March Madness: The Distinction of Men & Women"

raw_comment: After taking a look at the Twenty-Twenty Three NCAA basketball brackets, it surprises me that Iowa was the highest seeded team that made it to the championship game while being in the number two seed. By analyzing the graph, it can be seen that a team can win any game against one another no matter their rankings coming into the tournament. Every game starts with the score of zero to zero and any outcome is possible by the end. It is wondered what the percent chances were of LSU winning the women’s bracket and Connecticut winning the men’s bracket before the tournament started. The wins definitely were not predicted by their seeding, but there was surely some percentage calibrated for whether or not they could possibly win the tournament. The tournaments really don’t affect my community directly seeing as I am not closely affiliated with the college basketball world. However, the outcomes of games throughout the tournament go to show that in the general world of sports, meaning club, high school, or professional sports, there is always a chance of anything happening throughout a game and even the most confidently predicted results are never guaranteed. In the end, a catchy headline that would capture the graphs main idea would be, “Tournament of the Year.”

raw_comment:
1) I notice that throughout the 126 games played, the men's bracket generally seemed more volatile. In the final four, there was a 9th seed team, a 4th seed team, and two 5th seed teams. In comparison, the men's bracket had two 1st seed teams, a 2nd seed team, and a 3rd seed team, which are results that are much more expected. This means that the men's bracket had more upsets, and more underdog teams were able to make it to the semi-finals. 

2) I wonder what data is used to determine the seeding of the different teams? Do they use a single, specific value, like the points scored in previous games, or do they look at a number of factors like the previous results of the team and the lineup of players?  

3) Although I'm not a basketball fan personally, it is a popular sport in the community, and being able to understand what goes on in bracket graphs can help me connect with athletes in my community. 

4) March Madness Mayhem!

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
In this graph I notice in the mens bracket Connecticut won and they are the 4th seed and in the woman bracket LSU won and they're the third seed. The teams in the women's bracket seemed a little bit more expected to me than the ones in the men's.  The Final Four included two number 1 seeds, and the number two seed vs the number three seed matchup served as the championship game. 

What do I wonder?
I wonder why both the mens and the womans #1 seeds lost to Miami? As someone who isn't really aware of basketball and the terms, how do these seeds even get determined? Once the top seed has lost, does it get replaced by the victorious competitor? Also, I wonder if gender has anything to do with the stats of this graph.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because as every school does, my school has a basketball team. These stats are similar to the stats at my school where the girls basketball team dominates the boys basketball team. 

Create a catchy headline.
"Bracket Madness in March"

raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed is how complicated March Madness REALLY is. I thought it was just... basketball. But with this graph, now I know that it's a lot more. There are hundreds of teams from around the nation. The graph supports that because there are four sections that teams are split into - Greenville 1+2 and Seattle 1+2 for women, and Midwest, South, East, and West for men. 

I wonder why the scores increase across the board as the tournament progresses. Is it because teams drill harder the further they get into the tournament, or is it because offense/defense battles are more evenly matched? 

This relates to me and my community because most people in my community are big fans of Arkansas and wish they would've gotten further. 

This graph displays the winners/losers of each round and their scores during the tournament and leads all the way up to the final two.

What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

How does this relate to you and your community?

This relates to my community because March Madness is extremely popular. It’s also dependent on possible colleges and states.

raw_comment:
I notice that the top score for the final game in the women's bracket is higher than the top score in the men's bracket. 

I wonder about why that would happen. Could it be because of the rules, or because of the different body types, or even the different schools, or maybe different ways of coaching? 

This doesn’t necessarily relate to me now, but when I was younger I played in a basketball tournament and won the first year and came second the next. The community I am a part of now though, I don’t really get into the sports because I’m only going to be here for another year or so.

I think a good headline for this would be "Basketball Brackets Between (Genders and Scores)

Thanks to all students who responded.   Here are some of the great headlines:  “The March Madness Brackets that Drove Fans Mad” by Edy and “(Un)Predictable Madness: Men's and Women's March Madness Brackets” by Kai, both from California Polytechnic University San Luis Obispo; “2023: A Bracket Busting Year” by Ella and “Crave the Chaos: The Madness of the NCAA March Tournament” by Colleen, both from Academy of Saint Elizabeth in Morristown, New Jersey; and “NCAA March Madness 2023: Underestimated Underdogs Upset the Competition” by Daniel and “Bracket Madness: March's Historic Upsets and Victorious Joy” by Samuel, both from Perth Amboy High School in New Jersey.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, who marvels in sports that she cannot do, and Josh Tabor from Jackson, Tennessee, who once won a march-madness bracket competition by picking the teams from the most boring areas, who should have fewer distractions and more time to practice.

raw_comment:
1. My first reaction to this graph is how detailed it is. I noticed (and hardly ever realized) how competitive March Madness is. Total of 126 games were split by 64 men's teams and 64 women's teams. I see that Miami in both men's and women's tournaments made it to the quarterfinals. Also, the women's final game was higher than the men's final game. Looking at the graph overall, the lower number of seeds usually ends up winning the matches. 

2. I wonder how seeds are assigned as well as the concept as to why they exist in March Madness in the first place. Something that I also found quite interesting is the first four teams that played were in a separate bracket. Why is that? 

3. This relates to my community as I know March Madness fans who discuss seedings and how I honestly never fully understood what they spoke about. Everyone knows what March Madness is, but when shown a graph like this, it takes a moment to process what is really showing.

4. March Madness 2023: How did it go?

raw_comment:
1. One thing I noticed was that on the women's side, there were typically rather large point differences between the various bracketed teams, whereas on the men's side, the margins were typically fairly modest. The majority of the winning teams were from regions in either the midwest or east of the United States, which was something else I observed. Although there may not be much of a difference, I noted that the winning teams for both the men's and women's competitions came from eastern states like Louisiana and Connecticut.

2. I wonder whether there is a regional difference in how close some games are in addition to a gender difference in the point margins. Perhaps it has to do with the popularity of the team, the size of the city where the games are held, or whether or not the team plays on its home court. I wonder if any of these variables could have an impact on the point margins.

3. This relates to my community because I come from an area where basketball is a prominent sport in which it is played by both male and female. 

4. "March Madness Ends in an Epic Bracket Buster"

raw_comment:
-I observe that the brackets show the equal number of guys and females from the March Madness tournament. The grading for women and males differs and varies more on the female side. In the women's bracket, South Carolina placed first among the first four teams, with L.S.U coming in third despite having more points. The game had a first four because of the amount of teams. The seeding of males and females changed, with the top doing better and the bottom performing worse each time. Not every team made it over to March Madness. 

-I'm curious how much the team members' heights differed between teams. I'm also curious in how the teams are seeded, and what considerations are used. I'm interested in learning more about basketball scoring. 

-This is relevant to my community since this sport is popular among many kids at my school. Similar to how a lot of people pay attention to the March Madness in my town. Furthermore, I will be starting college soon, and this will be one of the numerous hobbies and sports available, so learning about the scoring may help me comprehend it better.

- Women’s vs. Men’s NCAA Basketball: WHO DOES IT BEST?

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I first noticed that from the round of 16 onward, the women’s bracket overall had more points scored per game than the men’s bracket. I also noticed the category saying the first four that were placed separate from the bracket at the bottom of each bracket. I also noticed that each state team had a seed and found it surprising that in one case, the number one seed was beaten by the eighth (Kansas vs Arkansas).

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the first four teams that played weren’t included in the bracket and were instead separated from it. I also wonder what the seedings for the tournaments were based on considering that in some cases, teams that had a lower seed than the other team ended up winning. And I also wonder why some states don’t have representation for both genders such as Alabama.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I because basketball is very popular among the students in school. And although I don’t play basketball very often I still find it enjoyable to play and watch every once in a while.

raw_comment:
The graphs display the scores for both the men and women's most recent "March Madness." The brackets include the dates of the games as well as the final scores for each game. I notice the women's winning team had a higher final score than the men.  

I wonder what caused the higher score for the women, if I were to not know anything about the sport and look at the graph my assumption would be that the women's team is much better than the men's team. But this could be that both men's teams had great defense, or that the women's team had a better offense than their opponents.

Basketball is a loved sport in my community, many students in my high school follow the sport, and or grew up playing it. Basketball and a lot of players are what motivate a lot of young people because their idols show them that they can be exemplary at something, even if they aren't at the moment.

March Madness ends in a slam dunk

Notice:
Both of these charts display the women’s and men’s brackets from the most recent March Madness. The charts display the points for each game as well as the rank of each of the schools. The bracket also labels each of the rounds and provides the dates which they had occurred above the matches. 

Wonder: 
I wonder how each of these teams are ranked before the tournament. I wonder why none of the teams which were ranked first were able to make it into the bracket, if they were predetermined to be the best. 

Observed:
I observed that while both teams had upsets within their brackets, the women’s brackets seemed to be much more consistent with rank. For instance, the final four of the women’s bracket included teams ranked: 1, 2, 1, and 3. However, the men’s final four consisted of lower ranked teams: 5, 9, 4, and 5. This indicates that the men’s bracket had more upsets in their bracket leading to lower ranked teams reaching the final four. I also observed that both of the teams that reached the final in both the men’s and women’s bracket were only one rank apart, with the women’s final being between teams ranked 2 and 3, and the men’s being 3 and 4. This resulted in a fairly evenly matched game.

The majority of the colleges that qualified for the Men's March Madness did not qualify for the Women's, and vice versa, I saw in this graph. I also saw that LSU and Connecticut, the two winning teams, both had greater saws than average.

This affects me because all of my family and friends watch the tournaments and fill out brackets. I take in a handful of the tournament's games as well. 

Title:  basketball bonanza

raw_comment:
I noticed that both graphs have the same general format, with 64 initial teams cut in half each round. The seed numbers are also identical because there are four groups of 1-16. I also noticed that the teams are separated into four different regions, which are different for the women’s and men’s brackets. In the men’s bracket, the regions are south, east, midwest, and west. However, in the women’s bracket, they are separated into Greenville 1, Greenville 2, Seattle 3, and Seattle 4.

I wonder how the teams are placed into their corresponding seeds. For example, what makes the team have to play in the “First Four” group? Why do they have to play an extra game when the NCAA can select 64 teams? Also, where are all the games played? With so many teams and games, they must spread out the games to accommodate everyone. I also wonder how often lower seeds beat the higher seeds in general.

I am going to be a college freshman in the fall and I am interested in how well my college's sports performances are compared to other universities in the state. This graph made me realize how competitive college sports are and why many students become very excited when their college sports team makes it into the Final Four.   

“Madness Unleashed: Tracing NCAA Basketball”

raw_comment:
I noticed in this graph that a lot of the schools that made it to the Men's March Madness did not make it to the Women's, and vice versa. I also noticed that both teams that won had a higher seen, LSU being third and Connecticut being 4.

I wonder why more people care and tune into the men's tournament than the women's. I also wonder if there is a reason some schools make it into one tournament and not the other.

This relates to me because my friends and family all tune into the tournaments as well as make brackets. I also watch a few games of the tournament.

This graph shows the Men's and Women's brackets from March Madness 2023. I noticed that teams that were in the higher seeds tended to do better. The team who won in the women's bracket was LSU which was third in the seed. And for the men's bracket Conneticut won, who was fourth in the seed. 

I wonder what causes upsets during the tournament. Were there injured players, bad calles made by the ref, etc.? 

This relates to me because many people in my community follow March Madness and make their own brackets. The results of the tournament are highly discussed.

raw_comment:
What do I notice? 
- In the final four and the final, the teams are very different for the men's teams versus the women's teams. 
- Depending on the college, the seed can be very similar for both the men's and women's teams. However, there are many where the seed is drastically different depending on whether it is the men's or women's team. 
- Mississippi State was in the first four for both the men's and women's teams. 
What do I wonder? 
- How exactly are the seeds calculated at the beginning of the year? 
- What leads to some of the seeds for the men's versus women's teams of the same colleges being so different? 
- Were there parts of the seed last year which are drastically different from this year's? 
What do I think is going on in this graph? 
- This graph is showing both the men's and women's college basketball NCAA 2023 bracket. The bracket provides both the initial seeds for all teams, and also the scores of the games. 
How does this relate to you and your community? 
- This relates to me and my community since, while basketball seems to be important where I live, a lot of people root for teams out of state. However, once a team in my area started doing very well (Fairleigh Dickinson), everyone in my area seemed to be rooting for them.

raw_comment: I noticed that the women's bracket had slightly more predictable teams than the men's. Two number 1 seeds were in the Final Four, and the Championship game was played between the number 2 seed and the number 3 seed. I noticed a few upsets at the beginning of the tournament, but the championship match had the top teams in the country. What's very interesting is that this is the first year since 1985 that Stanford, UCONN, or Tennessee has not been in the Elite Eight. I wonder what this will mean for collegiate women's basketball growth in America. This bracket shows the growth of the game away from just the perennially dominant teams such as UCONN, Stanford, and Tennessee and towards up-and-coming programs such as South Carolina, LSU, and Iowa. The men's bracket had many more upsets, like FDU and Princeton. No number one seed was left in the tournament by the elite eight. The final four for last year’s tournament were Kansas, UNC, Villanova, and Duke, teams that are usually at the top of the NCAA. This year's final four consisted of San Diego State, Florida Atlantic University, UCONN, and Miami. Besides Connecticut, most of these teams rarely advanced to the Elite Eight. How will this affect college basketball and the transfer portal? Will dominant teams in the NCAA change dramatically or gradually? This affects me because I am a fan of men’s and women’s college basketball. My headline is “Crave the Chaos: the Madness of the NCAA March Tournament.”

raw_comment:
These charts depict the 2023 NCAA March Madness brackets for men and women. From outside knowledge, I know that this year had a lot of upsets and surprises during the tournament. 16 seed FDU beat 1 seed Purdue in the men’s tournament, and for the women’s tournament, 9 seed Miami beat 1 seed Indiana—a complete surprise. I noticed that there were definitely more upsets in the men’s tournament compared to the women’s tournament. I wonder what causes these upsets, and I wonder how they rank these teams. I discovered that there really is no way to accurately predict what will happen during this tournament. This connects to me and my community because basketball is a very popular sport and March Madness has a very large viewing. 
Headline: The Best Ballers

1. One bracket is for the NCAA women's tournament, and the other is for the NCAA men's bracket. Additionally, the men's games scored more points overall than the women's games. As shown by the number of times higher-seeded teams defeated lower-seeded, considered to be more competent, teams, I've noticed that the men's bracket has more upsets than the women's bracket. For example, in the men's division, SDSU defeated Alabama, the first seed, by 7 points, while UConn defeated Gonzaga, the third seed, by 24 points. 

2. I'm curious as to why the names of the teams and where they are from different. Why do males teams typically play for big cities while women generally play for their states? Did they carry out this action in order to separate the brackets while reporting the score?

3. This relates to me and my community because a good number of people love basketball and this information is something that would probably peak their interest.

4. March Madness is Causing Madness

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  
Today’s graphs are the final brackets for the 2023 March Madness.  No one had a perfect bracket – selecting all of the winners of either the women’s or men’s championships.
From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online for the four questions.  We have added a suggestion to the “What do you notice?” question.  If your notice includes a claim, please back it up with evidence that supports your claim.  
By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the free link to the online article that included these graphs.  

You can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

The next graph will be released by Friday, April 21 with moderation on Wednesday, April 26.  The topic – sex education.

raw_comment:
I noticed that lower seeded teams had lots of upsets in the Men's tournament. Teams like Princeton and FDU beat 2 and 1 seeded teams. None of the 1 seeded teams made it to the Final Four, and a 4 seed, UConn, won the tournament. However, in the women's tournament there was not as many large upsets, but the 3 seeded team, LSU, did win. I wonder why there was so many crazy upsets in the men's tournament this year. Why did the higher seeds not have success? This relates to my community because FDU is right around me and they are the second 16 seed to beat a 1 seed in tournament history. 

2023: A Bracket Busting Year

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that more commonly in the Men's Bracket various low seeded teams upset higher seed like Princeton's Historic run where they overcame the 2 seed Arizona and 7 seed Missouri as the 15 seed or Fla Atlantic's run to the semi-finals as a 9 seed. even Sand Diego's run to the finals beating out Alabama the 1 seed as the 5 seed and their opponent in the final Connecticut being a 4 seed making the March Madness Brackets almost impossible to guess for how many upsets or unexpected victories their were for these lower seeds.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how much a one game elimination affects these games scores? 
How different would it be if it were like the NBA 7 game series?
DId Injuries or other factors stop top seeds making it to the finals?

How does this relate to you and your community?
Especially this year with the incredible amounts of upsets and with Princeton and FDU taking part in March Madness and being from New Jersey and in the Fall being a incoming Freshman It was honestly inspiration to see them overcome their seeding to make historic runs in the tournament taking a piece of their run to serve as motivation for the future ahead as no matter if i'm counted out or facing adversity I can overcome.

raw_comment: This graph demonstrates the NCAA Men's and Women's March Madness brackets.  The main thing I notice is how in both brackets, relatively higher seeded teams got to the finals.  In women's, it was 2 seed Iowa and 3 seed LSU, and in the men's it was 5 seed S.D. State and 4 seed Connecticut.  Additionally, the different sides have comparable scores for most games.  There is a good variety of close games, as well as clear wins.  However, one thing that does stand out is how the women's final had a rather high scoring game and the men's final was much lower.  I wonder how exactly they rank all the teams.  Some teams have better records than others, but are still being ranked lower.  Could this be because they played against harder competition or won more games in their division?  This affects me and my community because college basketball is a popular form of entertainment and is something many my age pay a lot of attention to.  I would entitle this graph: "Expanding on March Madness."

raw_comment:
I thought it was interesting how the records didn't determine the rankings for both brackets. Some examples of this includes Charleston being seed 12 with a 31-3 record and SDSU being seed 5 with a worse 27-6 record for the men's side. Similarly, one the women's side, Gardner Webb had a better record than Utah (29-4, 25-4 respectively), but Gardner was ranked 15th and Utah was ranked 2nd.  It was also interesting how that both brackets had the same number of upsets in the round of 64 (7) and similar upsets in the round of 32 (4 for women and 5 for men), the men had a much lower average ranking in the sweet 16 than the women. The men's average ranking is 4.875, while the womens is a 3.69.

One thing I wonder about is how the teams are ranked. As mentioned above, teams with worse records are ranked higher, so I wonder what the algorithm is to determine this. What other factors are in play when determining the team rankings?

This relates to me as I filled out a March Madness bracket myself. While I did pretty poorly, I think brackets are fun, as it provides a light hearted competition and can connect you to the game, even if you don't care about basketball. I personally find sports boring, but I still would constantly check for results and rooting for teams in my bracket.

A headline for this graph could be "Decoding the March Madness"

raw_comment:
After looking at the NCAA bracket results, I noticed that the Men's tournament had many upsets, and top-ranked teams missed the second round. I wonder how many games were decided by pure chance, not from superior skill or talent. For example, San Diego State University had two consecutive game-winning shots in the quarter and semi-finals. If you look at the Women's tournament, the higher-seeded teams generally prevailed hence fewer upsets. For example, seven of the eight teams in the elite were ranked seed five or below. Additionally, I wonder how these outcomes would change if the tournament was longer and each round had a series of games. March Madness was fun to watch because I like playing and watching basketball in general, and I have roommates from San Diego who were San Diego State fans. Overall, this bracket encaptures how the Men's and Women's tournaments unfolded. Each team was assigned a tournament seed from strength of schedule and regular season record. I am excited to watch March Madness again next year!

raw_comment:
I notice that for the women’s bracket the first round of games (Round of 64) a majority of games have a big score difference unlike the first round of games for the men’s bracket. In the Women’s bracket 18 out of 32 games have at least a 20 point difference as seen in Maryland (93) vs. Holy Cross (61). Unlike the Women’s bracket,  only 6 out of 32 games have at least a 20 point difference as shown in Kansas (96) vs. Howard (68). 

I wonder how the total number of people in the audience has an effect on the outcome of the game. Will more people create a larger difference in the final score? Do smaller teams do better with a smaller audience?

This relates to my community because March Madness has been going on for years. I remember in middle school and high school, talking about teams with my friends and teachers. When I was younger March Madness brought a lot of people together and still continues to do so today by encouraging others to show team spirit.

This graph shows the outcomes of every game in March Madness including the team names, round number, and final score. I believe a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea is “Making Moves and Buckets in March Madness”.

raw_comment:
What did I notice?:

Something that I noticed first in the women's bracket is that the teams with a high seeding in each group ended up advancing further than the lower-seeded teams in their group bracket.  For example in the final four, the highest seed was 1 and the lowest was 3 which is very impressive.  Most of the scores from both brackets were really close games and there weren't many blowouts.  In the women's bracket, there were also only two games where a team scored over 100 points.  In the men's bracket, there were no games that reached 100.  The highest-scoring game was 98 put up by Kansas State in the game versus Michigan State in the elite eight games for the East group.

What do I wonder?:

I wonder how each team is seeded because initially, I thought it was just the team's record from the season, but it seems like some teams are seeded lower than other teams but they have a better record.  For example in the women's bracket, the Seattle 4 region, Middle Tenn. has a record (28-4) but is seed eleven and Colorado has a record (23-8) as the sixth seed.  

How does this relate to you and your community?:

I do play basketball and watch basketball occasionally.  March Madness is actually something I did watch as it was happening.  I kept up with a few teams and It was fun to see future NBA prospects and these young players going at it with each other.  It's very intense and exciting.

raw_comment:
From comparing the final four for both the women's and men's bracket, it's interesting to see the difference in the seeding of the teams. From the women's bracket, the final four consisted of higher seeding teams competing such as seeding #1 through #3, while the men's final four consisted of teams such as Fla. Atlantic, which was seed #9. It is also interesting to see that in both brackets, teams that were seed #1 did not win the championship even though in the women's bracket, two seed #1 teams made it to the final four. What I wondered as I analyzed the brackets was how teams were seeded. In the men's bracket, why is USC seeded in the Eastern region when it should be seeded in the West? Why is Northwestern playing in the Western Conference? Is it because the school is North"west"ern? 

March Madness was very entertaining to watch and engage in since my friends and I would create brackets and predict the winning team. However, my predictions would always fall short since the games are unpredictable and the outcomes are unexpected. Overall, March Madness is a bonding experience between my friends and I and we usually look forward to it every year. 

Catchy Headline: Madness in March

raw_comment:
After looking at the round of 64, I noticed that that was the category that played the outermost ranked teams (rank #1 v rank #16, rank #2 v rank #15, and so on). After observing them I noticed that the more extreme female teams tended to have a larger spread in points compared to the more extreme male teams. After observing this data I recorded the point and averaged the 8 most largest ranked unbalanced games. The mean difference in scores between the 8 sets of women's' games was a point difference of 35.375 points while the mean difference in scores between the 8 sets of men's games was a point difference of 17.375. We can also observe that all of the sampled individual mens game differences fall beneath the women's point difference mean (35.375) and all of the sampled individual women's games fall above the men's point difference mean (17.375).

This makes me wonder why there is such an extreme difference in points. A larger mean difference in points would most likely mean that the variance in skill is higher. (Although my sport's knowledge is limited) I suspect that the higher viewership and profits give incentive for mens basketball to be a more competitive environment leading to a potential smaller variance in point spreads. 

More than half of my friends follow March Madness and enjoy watching the games. Although I am not as invested, it is interesting to see the games as a whole after they have been played through.

Whats going on in this graph?

A Spread in Skills

raw_comment:
From the brackets of the men’s and women’s NCAA 2023 basketball tournament, I see that the brackets seem to be organized based on geographical divisions, with named divisions which are different for the men’s and women’s teams. Both the men’s and women’s brackets are organized by regions. The brackets are also aesthetically pleasing due to the placement of headers above each round (e.g. “Round of 64”) along with dates so the timeline of the games are easier to follow. 
Something that could be added to make the visualization clearer is a key to the numbers on either side of each school’s name, so the viewer knows whether these are initial rankings, randomly assigned team numbers, or any other meaningful number. I’m also left wondering what the “First Four” means. These questions are more relevant for readers like myself who don’t follow basketball.
While I don’t actively follow basketball, March Madness is still a huge phenomenon for college students like myself. My brother is also a huge fan of March Madness and he attended SDSU and talked to me a lot about the games.
Based on the information conveyed in the visual, this could be titled “Breaking into the Brackets: LSU and Connecticut Bring it Home”

raw_comment:
For the men's final four, they were given 5 days after their round of 8 while the women's final four only had 3 days after their round of 8 before final four.  Miami made it to round of 8 for both men's and women's, the farthest a schools placed for both their teams in 2023 N.C.A.A. Lower seeded teams can very well be passed by lower seeded teams. For men's, Connecticut(4th) went against Delaware State (5th). For women's all 1st seeds also got out and both Iowa(2nd) and L.S.U(3rd) went against each other. The regions they use differ, women's used the Greenville area as 1 and 2 and Seattle area as 3 and 4 and men's uses north south east west. Princeton for being seed 15 still made it to round 16 which was impressive. 

What would the results be if Women's L.S.U. and men's Connecticut who both won the NCAA tournament this year went against each other? Why did men's tournament have a 5 day period between round of 8ths and final four while women's had 3 days. Did change in coaches or injured players change the results, who would've been higher or lower?

It's senior year for me so people going into athletics and pursuing a career in basketball could look at a schools performance in the N.C.A.A. tournament this year and make a college decision based off it and who they think they'd work best with and benefit from. N.C.A.A. tournaments are also popular and serve as entertainment for many, myself included.

Best Ballers: L.S.U and UCONN Ball Out to Victory Again

1. 

 I notice that the champions of both the women's bracket and the men's bracket do not have seed #1. In the Final Four of the Men's bracket, there does not have any team that has seed #1 while there are two teams in the Final Four of the Women's bracket that have seed #1. Overall, teams of the Final Fours of the Women's bracket have higher seed rankings than the teams of the Final Fours of the Men's bracket since all four Women's bracket teams have seed rankings from range #1 to #3 while all four Men's bracket teams have seed rankings outside of the #1 to #3 range. It is interesting to find out that the seed ranking is not always necessarily a good prediction of how well a team may perform. 

2. 

I am interested in knowing how the seed ranking level was determined. It is based on the past performance of the team in the previous March Madness competitions? Will a team's seed ranking drop if they have a bad performance in the current March Madness competition? 

3. 
I am a college student and I am interested in how well my college's sports performances are compared to other universities in the state. I have known students that will lose interest in college sports if they knew their college did not have good sports performances. This graph made me realize how competitive college sports are and why many students become very excited when their college sports team makes it into the Final Four. 

4. 
"March Madness Had Ended After a Long Battle with Both Sweat and Tears "

raw_comment:
One aspect that I took notice of were the number of upsets in both the men and women's brackets. Neither of them had number one seeds in the final, and in the men's bracket the last of the number one seeds were knocked out in the round of 16, so not a single number one seed remained in the last 8 teams of the tournament. 

I wonder how often it is that number one or even two seed make it to the final four, or better.  Something else I'm curious about is how seeds are determined. I know that the team's record plays a big role in that, but an example where even that doesn't hold is when San Diego St. is seeded 5th with a (27-6) record, and they play a 12th seeded Charleston team (31-3). Even though Charleston has 4 more wins, they are seeded 7 places below San Diego St. It would be cool to know how much other factors play into seeding for March Madness. 

As for an impact on the community, I think that all of these upsets and seemingly unpredictable factors that happen in games adds elements of thrill and excitement to make for more attention and viewers during the tournament.

raw_comment:
I noticed how there are six rounds of games for the entirety of March Madness for both men’s and women’s basketball, not counting the first four games shown at the bottom of the graphs. They each start with 64 teams, each assigned an initial seed. The men’s bracket is grouped by simple regions while the women’s bracket is grouped by Greenville or Seattle, numbered 1-4. I also noticed that the team’s previous stats were noted next to the team name in the first round, except for almost all the 16 seed teams. However, one 16th seed team beat the 1st seed in the men's bracket, which I thought was interesting. 
I wonder why they match up the teams in the first round the way that they do. It almost seems unfair to set the 16th seed team against the 1st seed team right off the bat. I wonder if it would be better to pair 1 with 9 and 2 with 10 and so on for the first games. Also, I would like to learn what the region grouping means for the women’s bracket, because I could not quite grasp it from the graph. I am also curious about how many people guessed these exact brackets before march madness started. 

This impacts me and my community because my school was not in a league that participated in the displayed March Madness bracket and I wish my school was good enough to be included.

My catchy headline would be: “Brack Attack! Madness is in the Air!”

raw_comment:
I really enjoy how these graphs organize a lot of information in a really concise and clear way. I can see that the way they determine who plays who in the first games starts by pairing the highest and lowest seeds and then working inward (2-15, 3-14, etc). However, I wonder how they decide what order these original games will be placed in the bracket because the original placement determines much of who they play in future games. I can infer the sorting of the original games and team seeds stay constant due to it being the same between womens and mens brackets. I think these graphs show just how big of a deal March Madness and sports are as America's favorite pastime. A ton of people make their own prediction brackets just like these and anxiously tune in to watch and root for their picks. 
I think a fun headline would be “Did your March Madness Bracket Make it or Bust?”

raw_comment:
It's interesting how, in the women's brackets, Virginia Tech and South Carolina both made it to the final four, and they were initially seed #1 in their respective initial divisions. However, neither team advanced to the championship. It's also interesting how the two championship teams were fairly matched in seed levels. Iowa was seed #2, and LSU was seed #3 in their respective initial divisions. A similar thing is seen in the men's bracket, where SD state was seed #5, and Connecticut was seed #4 in their respective initial divisions. It's intriguing to see how the teams that were initially given top-seed values due to their superior performance maintained their performance and were ultimately evenly matched in the final game. However, the teams given the #1 seed value, to begin with, don't seem to make it into the championship. I wonder how often a #1 seeded team makes it to the championship and, moreover, actually becomes champion. 

Being a college student with friends who love and play basketball, this is not the first time I have heard about March Madness. It's fun to recognize a few familiar teams on the bracket, like UCSB and UCLA. Although I am not a diehard basketball fan, joining a community and supporting your peers is fun.
Happy March Madness!

raw_comment:
I noticed that the women's Final Four featured only teams seeded first through third in their divisions, while the men's Final Four featured more underdog teams such as FAU who were ranked ninth in their division. I also noticed that teams were in some cases seeded higher than teams with better overall records in the regular season.
I wonder how the selection committee decides how teams should be seeded. Does the name of the college sometimes cause bias in the decisions? Also, I wonder why the location of the schools does not seem to be in line with the region they are placed in, with teams like USC being in the "East" region.
Personally, I enjoy watching March Madness and filling out my own bracket predictions. The unpredictability and chaos that the games bring is very fun to watch.

raw_comment: From the March Madness Bracket, I notice that many of the higher-seeded teams (especially seeds 1 or 2), didn't make it to the elite 8 for both the men's and women's side of the brackets.  Only five of the 16 teams that fit the above criteria actually made the elite 8, which is much lower than I had expected.  I also noticed that the women's bracket final scored far more points than the men's bracket final.  This leads me to wonder why we found this to be true.  Were the defenses in the men's final that much more dominant?  Or were the offenses of the women's final that much more efficient?  As a college student who is involved in the big 3 North American sports, I was heavily invested in this year's March Madness.  It was very tough to watch the teams I had picked to win (UCLA and Purdue) lose in the ways they did.  A catchy headline for this graph could be: "Mulitverse of Madness!  How the Men's and Women's Brackets Ended!"

raw_comment:
I noticed that the regional groups for the women's bracket followed cities while the regional groups for the men's bracket were general directions. Also the dates of the different rounds were slightly different between the 2 brackets. The women's bracket starts a day later than the men's and has the final a day earlier than the men's . I also notice that in the men's bracket, the round of 8 included more lower seeded teams than the women's bracket.

I wonder how the first 4 works. Why are teams that are seeded 11 playing these preliminary games when teams ranked 12-15 are not? I also noticed that Miami was the only team the preformed well in both brackets. why is this? I would think that there would be more similarity between men and women's teams in terms of how well thy both preform. A good women's basketball program doesn't necessarily mean that the school also has a good men's basketball program. Why? I also wonder why the number of games played by teams vary so much. For the most part teams have between 30 and 34 games played, however, Hawaii only has 22 games played. Im sure this has something to do with how far away Hawaii is, however, this difference doesn't seem fair.

This graph related to me and my community because, I go to a university that has both men and women's basketball.

raw_comment:
What Do you Notice?

I noticed that both graphs have the same general format, with 64 initial teams that are cut in half each round. The seed numbers are also identical because there are four groups of 1-16. I also noticed that the teams are separated into four different regions, which are different for the women’s and men’s brackets. In the men’s bracket, the regions are south, east, midwest, and west. However, in the women’s bracket, they are separated into Greenville 1, Greenville 2, Seattle 3, and Seattle 4.

What do you wonder?

I wonder how the teams are placed into their corresponding seeds. For example, what makes a team have to play in the “First Four” group? raw_comment:
What do you notice?
From the graph, I first noticed that there are two brackets, a women’s bracket, and a men’s bracket. I also notice that there is more to the graph than just the winning teams, there is also additional information about the games and teams at the top and bottom of the graph. For example, the dates for each of the games are labeled at the top for each bracket, as well as “The First Four.” This is a cool feature that is included. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the black bars on the side are different for the women’s bracket and the men’s bracket. I also wonder what some of the numbers mean, would there be a way to put a legend of some sort? 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
I personally do not watch basketball very often, but many of my friends and family members do. They like to put sports bets and watch every game. Especially being a college student, many of my peers fill out their own brackets. 

What is a catchy headline that captures “what’s going on this graph”?
“Madness Unleashed: Tracing NCAA Basketball”

1.  I notice that at the center of the championships, the men's score of the winning team is significantly less than that of the women's team, the scores being 102 vs. 76. I also notice that some schools dominate more in one team rather than the other. For example, Princeton played better in the men's team with 75 points in the round of 16 while the women's team got 56 in the round of 32. On the other hand, Iowa lost in the round of 64 for the men's bracket while getting to the finals in the women's bracket. 

2. I wonder if the players' upbringing and financial situation have any bearing on how motivated they are to win games.  

3. Most of the sports at my school have both male and female teams, and some teams from the same sport simply perform better than their counterparts. 

4.  "Bracket Madness; Men's and Women's Basketball Tournaments"

raw_comment:
I notice that both the men’s and women’s brackets are laid out the same, with the round labels at the top, the label in the center, each team with the respective points and seed per game, and the final match in gray in the center. I also notice that for the women’s team final, the seeds are 2 and 3, which seems very likely. However the men’s final has a fourth and fifth seed, which means there must have been a few upsets during the tournament.

Seeing a visualization of the final bracket shows me how many first-pick teams had upset and how exciting the season must have been. 
I would title this: “March Madness: A Wild Season Broken Down”.

raw_comment:
I noticed that of the 16 teams in the elite eight of both the men's and women’s teams, only a single 1 seed team remained and there was no 1 seed team in either championship game. I also noticed that it seemed that the women’s teams scored higher than the men’s teams overall with higher maximum scores.
I wonder how normal it is for 1 seed to lose early, specifically in the first round. I also wonder how many people have perfectly predicted a march madness bracket.
As a college student who enjoys playing and watching basketball, this affects me and my community of friends. Although I am not super into march madness, I will often fill out a bracket for fun.
A catchy headline could be: “Finding the Method to the Madness”

raw_comment:
1) This graphic has two different brackets, one for the NCAA women's tournament and one for the NCAA men's bracket. Furthermore, the women's games scored fewer overall points than the men's games. I've noticed that the men's bracket has more upsets than the women's bracket, as seen by the number of occasions on which higher-seeded teams defeated lower-seeded, perceived to be more competent, teams; in the men's division, SDSU defeated Alabama (1st seed) by 7 points, while UConn defeated Gonzaga (3rd seed) by 24 points. 

2) I wonder if certain players being substituted during the games played a role in a team's placement. I wonder if the brackets from previous years illustrate trends for certain groups in distinct divisions. Regarding the number of upsets in the divisions, I question the legitimacy of the seedings, and whether these upsets will have a cascade effect, impacting the seedings for the following year.

3) This has an impact on my community since many students and citizens in the community watch college basketball and like predicting brackets, and these charts demonstrate how difficult it is to make a reliable prediction. Analyzing the data for the games and realizing trends allows people to make more accurate predictions. There are some universities near my area that have participated in March Madness, a stage that students aspire to reach.

4) NCAA March Madness 2023: Underestimated Underdogs Upset the Competition

raw_comment:
1. First thing that I noticed was that the winning team on both the Men's and Women's bracket scored significantly less on their semifinal game compared to their final winning score. I also noticed that all 4 #1 ranked teams advanced in the competition in the Women's Bracket, but not in the Men's bracket.

I wonder if there could be some other statistic that could be taken into consideration that will give us more information on playoff performance. I know ranking has to do with games won, but not every team is built for playoffs, so it would be cool to see if there was a way to factor this into rankings.

As a statistic student, this is relevant to those students that want to establish a career in the sports world.

March Madness Magic: The Thrill of the Bracket

raw_comment:
I noticed that the seeding occurs in ranks numbered 1 to 16. I could be wrong as to how the process works, but I find it odd that ranks 1 and 16 are placed against each other in every region. This feels like a way to weed out the 16th, but maybe that is the point, they might not want many close games at the start. It also results in games between teams that are closer in skill towards the end. 

I wonder how the ranks are decided and how accurate they tend to be. Additionally, I wonder how they decide both where these games are held, and the four regions of the brackets. I wonder how that affects the assignment of ranks, as well as if two teams of the same rank have ever gone against each other before the Final Four.

This does not relate to me much as I am not actively following basketball, however I have friends who want to go into a career of analyzing sports statistics.

A catchy headline might be "2023 N.C.A.A. March Madness Results"

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that for both brackets, the championship game didn’t feature any #1 seeds, but rather matchups between the 2 vs 3 seed and the 4 vs 5 seed. In addition, the women’s games were typically played one day after the men’s for each round (Round of 64, 32, 16, etc…) and that the women’s games in the Final Four and Final had higher scores than the men in their respective games. 

2) I wonder if some sort of probability could have been added to the brackets/graphs that add context to how likely/unlikely a potential matchup or run might be. With this year in particular, it might be interesting to provide a figure that shows the probability of a lower seed forcing an upset and making it to the Final. 

3) These brackets represent an exciting set of games for sports fans to follow in March. I always enjoy filling out a bracket before March Madness and seeing just how quickly the predictions get busted. This was a unique and exciting year where lower seeds made some incredible and unexpected runs.

4) A potential name for this graph might be “The Madness of Brackets.”

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that for both brackets, the championship game didn’t feature any #1 seeds, but rather matchups between the 2 vs 3 seed and the 4 vs 5 seed. In addition, the women’s games were typically played one day after the men’s for each round (Round of 64, 32, 16, etc…) and that the women’s games in the Final Four and Final had higher scores than the men in their respective games. 

2) I wonder if some sort of probability could have been added to the brackets/graphs that add context to how likely/unlikely a potential matchup or run might be. With this year in particular, it might be interesting to provide a figure that shows the probability of a lower seed forcing an upset and making it to the Final. 

3) These brackets represent an exciting set of games for sports fans to follow in March. I always enjoy filling out a bracket before March Madness and seeing just how quickly the predictions get busted. This was a unique and exciting year where lower seeds made some incredible and unexpected runs.

4) A potential name for this graph might be “The Madness of Brackets.”

4) An "Even" Playing Field

raw_comment:
1) I notice that there are two brackets being shown, one side being the women's bracket and the other side being the men's bracket. These brackets show the results of the games that took place in the March Madness tournament. UConn was winning by bigger margins than SDSU in the men's bracket, which can lead us to anticipate that they would also win by a big margin against SDSU. UConn had also defeated No. 3 seed Gonzaga by 24 points, while SDSU defeated No. 1 seed Alabama by 7 points. Many of the games in the round of 64 were incredibly close, with most being decided by only three points. And for the women, LSU and Iowa were going into the championship game.

2) What I wonder is how much time it took to assemble the teams and create the bracket and if there's ever been an accurate bracket prediction made throughout the years.

3) This relates to me and my community since a big portion of the kids in my age group are into basketball especially now that the weather is getting nicer outside, there's more people outside playing.

4) Bracket the Madness

raw_comment:
I notice that neither of the championship games had a one seed. In both brackets, there were plenty of upsets that led to unexpected winners.

I wonder why there were so many upsets this year. Normally in March Madness, there are a lot of upsets, but once you get to the final four, you have three or four powerhouse teams that nobody was surprised to see. Maybe there was just more high quality teams this year which opened the door for non one-seeds to make deep runs.

My family and friends all make brackets and follow the tournaments closely even when our chances of winning money are near 0.

March Madness Lives up to its Name

raw_comment:
Both of these images are similar in the way that they contain the results of each game that has taken place in the March Madness tournament. At the beginning, each team plays another team. However, because this is a tournament, losing makes a team eliminated, which is why there are fewer seeds towards the middle of both brackets. The tournament culminates with a championship game.  

While both brackets are structured exactly the same, upon analyzing them, I discovered that very different teams ended up advancing in the tournament when comparing the men and women’s brackets. This leads me to wonder why certain schools have better women’s basketball teams than men’s basketball teams, or vice versa. Is the basketball program for one gender more likely to be good if the other gender’s program is not? Also, I am curious to know what the distribution of funding for both basketball programs are for a given school and how that may play into the quality of their teams. 

I have always been into basketball. I started playing when I was 8 and I competed all through high school. My dad also played basketball growing up, as he was both my brother and I’s inspiration to begin playing. Because basketball is a large part of our lives, we are always tuned in when March Madness is happening. Based on the teams’ performances throughout the year, we fill out brackets and make predictions accordingly. 

Men vs. Women’s Brackets: The Discrepancies

raw_comment:
One thing that I noticed is that one-sided women's games involved teams scoring much lower than one-sided men's games. For example, Virginia Tech vs Chattanooga in the first round of the women's bracket resultsed in a 58-33 win for Virginia Tech, a pretty low scoring game. However, the lower scoring games for some of the men's games hovered around 50 points, 1.5 times higher than the minimum for the women's games.

I wonder what the upset rate is for all NCAA March Madness games (i.e, a lower ranked team beating a higher ranked team), as I often hear of plenty of upsets that occur in this setting.

While I am not a huge basketball fan, plenty of colleges from my state participate in March Madness, thus many fans in my community tune in to support their teams. So, March Madness captures the interest of many in my community.

A catchy title I thought of is "The bracket no one made -- again" as the results of these games are often unpredictable.

I notice that no #1 seeds (the teams with the best odds to win the tournament) made it past the round of sixteen in the Men’s bracket, and that no #1 seeds made the finals in either bracket. 
What do I wonder?
I wonder why for the past couple of years, those big teams, with expectations to win the tournament, go out to smaller teams, we have seen Arkansas beat two #1 seeds two years in a row, but how? Is it that March Madness spirit?
How does this affect you or your community?
I would say that this directly affects my community (and me specifically) because me, and the people around me love the game of basketball. That March Madness time of year is always a hype year, even if your team gets knocked out, or didn’t make it.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the women’s final game resulted in higher scoring teams overall compared to the men’s: 102 to 85 for the women’s game, and 76 to 59 for the men’s final game as shown in the light grey box in the center of each bracket.

I wonder if there was a way to better distinguish which numbers represent a school’s seed ranking or their final score in a game. When reading the bracket, I only was quickly able to understand these numbers because I knew that Iowa and L.S.U. were the two schools that went to the women's finals and each of their seed rankings. It may be a more confusing graph for people who don’t understand NCAA seed rankings and watch basketball often.

I also wonder whether the final game of the women’s tournament had more viewers this year because with higher scores, a game is thought to be more exciting since there’s more action in the game. The media recently has taken a liking to Iowa’s point-guard Caitlyn Clark, which may have influenced the popularity of the women’s tournament this year in general.

I relate to this because I started watching this year’s women’s March Madness tournament when it got to the “Sweet Sixteen,” which is when there are only 16 teams left in the tournament.

raw_comment: What I notice from the graph it is an organized bracket of all of the basketball teams, both men's and women's. Each team is within its own bracket, which determines who will move forward based on if the team has won or not. Another thing I noticed was the date both men and women took their finals. The women were a day before the men's basketball team. I wonder if how many people were close to getting a perfect bracket? I also wonder how long it took to organize the teams and to set up the bracket. The impact that March Madness has on my environment is not as impactful, but it does bring in new hobbies for people to get into. I would say it is also a competition of who would be closest to getting a perfect bracket. What are the odds of getting a perfect bracket?

raw_comment:
1.I noticed that for Women's basketball, the games of the final four were very close in points and the winners were just a few points off. For the men's side, the midwest and west for the final four teams were very far apart in number of points. I also noticed that most of the schools on the women's roster are not on the men's basketball and vice versa. I noticed that in the final four for both genders the scores stayed in the 70s range but for the finals LSU had its big win with 102 points.  
2. I wonder how the march madness games can affect the ranking of the schools that are number 1 in their region and didn't end up at the top. I wonder how the schools that go against each other in the first round are chosen since they are all in different rankings. I also wonder if playing teams from your region affect who comes at the top from that region since those teams might have played each other before unlike playing someone from a different region in the first rounds. 
3. This relates to me and my community because some of the schools that are D1 in my state almost had a chance of being in the finals. Princeton was out in the round of 14 which was just three games away from finals. If Princeton were to bring the championship to the state, it would bring people in the state together. Getting a win like that for the state can make the other teams in Jersey train harder to continue to win in the future.
4. Teams of Men and Women Dribble Their Way To Bring The Trophy Home

raw_comment:
March Madness: Who Will Make It to the Final Four
I notice that some of the lower seeds of the men's bracket and the women's bracket ended up beating the higher seeds. For example, in the men's bracket, Fairleigh Dickinson was the 16th seed and their first game was against Purdue who was seeded 1, FDU won. Furthermore, in the women's bracket, Auburn was ranked #9 and Iowa was ranked #8, but Auburn had won. I wonder how some of these teams beat their higher seat, then lost to another team that was still seeded higher than them, but wasn't "as good" as the team they originally beat. This relates to my community because last yea our boys team had beat various teams that the WIAA had ranked higher than them and they ended up beating them, and also becoming 3A state champions. This graph is showing the completed men's and women's March Madness brackets with seeds and scores.

raw_comment:
The graph shows the match-ups and outcomes for each game in the 2023 NCAA basketball tournaments.  The only noticeable difference is the categories for which the tournament coordinators separated the teams in the first round.  The women’s bracket categories are Greenville 1, Greenville 2, Seattle 3, and Seattle 4 while the men’s bracket categories are South, Midwest, East, and West.  Another small difference is the duration for each tournament.  The men’s tournament was two days longer than the women’s tournament.  The graph’s most noticeable feature is the organization.  For each game, the graph shows the team names, score, standing, and game date.  The lines connecting the games provide an intuitive flow to indicate which team won and moved to the next round.  The graph highlights the championship game with a thick border.  I wonder why the women’s tournament categories are different, and how the coordinators chose the categories.  I play basketball, and our team created competing brackets, but Mississippi ruined my women’s bracket, and Princeton ruined my men’s bracket.  

Rankings, Scores, Championships: LSU and UCONN the Underestimated Champions

raw_comment:
1) One thing I notice is that in the men's bracket, UConn was winning by much larger margins than SDSU, which seemed to predict that they would also win against SDSU by a large margin. For example, SDSU beat 1 seed Alabama by a 7-point margin, while UConn beat 3 seed Gonzaga by a 24-point margin.

2) I wonder what made this UConn team so good in the playoffs, as they were only seeded 4th in their conference coming into the tournament.

3) This relates to me and my community because I am from San Diego and have been watching SDSU basketball since the 2010 season, so it was heartbreaking to see them lose in their only ever Finals appearance.

4) These visualizations compare seedings between matchups in the March Madness tournament, and displays the score outcome of each matchup along with the winner.

5) Marvelous Madness: A Year of Underdogs

raw_comment:
1.) One thing I noticed was there were usually pretty big point margins between the different bracketed teams on the women’s side, and fairly small point margins in most cases on the men’s side. Another thing I noticed was that the majority of the winning teams were from places in either the midwest or east in the U.S. This might not be that big of a difference, but I noticed that the winning teams from both the men and women were from eastern places in the U.S. (eg Louisiana and Connecticut). 

2.) I wonder if there is not only a gender difference in the point margins, but if there is a regional difference in how close different games are? Maybe it has to do with team popularity, how big the city the matches are played in, or whether or not the team plays at their home court or not. Maybe any number of these factors affect the point margins, I wonder.

3.) A lot of my friends are into basketball, and I’m certain they’ll find the scores and their differences interesting.

4.) Madness in March: The Intriguing Differences in March Madness scores for NCAA Basketball

1) One thing I notice is that in the men's bracket, UConn was winning by much larger margins than SDSU, which seemed to predict that they would also win against SDSU by a large margin. For example, SDSU beat 1 seed Alabama by a 7-point margin, while UConn beat 3 seed Gonzaga by a 24-point margin.

4) These visualizations compare seedings between matchups in the March Madness tournament, and displays the score outcome of each matchup along with the winner.

5) Marvelous Madness: A Year of Underdogs

raw_comment: I initially noticed that as each team is listed in the Round of 64, next to team name is their standings. The four teams from the First Four that make the top 64 do not have their standings included, but in the Women’s Bracket a fifth team, Norfolk State also does not have standings. In the Men’s Bracket, this does not occur seeing as the only four teams without their standings listed are the four teams from the First Four. One aspect of this graph that is excluded that I believe is critical to include is the year. I know that these brackets are for the 2023 N.C.A.A. basketball tournament, but that is not explicitly stated on the graph. As someone who grew up in the South, college sports are a huge deal. Specifically, college football and basketball. The March Madness bracket is the topic of discussion throughout the entire month of March, so these graphs have a huge impact on my community. As a college student, discussing March Madness brackets and watching the games are some of the most popular activities of the month. This month, more specifically for the men’s basketball, I was completely shocked by several games. Teams in high seeds were losing to much lower seed teams. I think a fitting name for this graph would be “The March Madness Brackets that Drove Fans Mad.”

1. **Chart type**  
   - Tournament bracket diagram for NCAA basketball, shown separately for **Women’s Bracket** and **Men’s Bracket**.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Side-by-side panels**: two large bracket panels, one for women and one for men.  
   - **Bracket/tree layout**: teams progress through rounds via connected lines.  
   - **Regional subdivision** within each bracket (e.g., Greenville, Seattle, South, East, Midwest, West).  
   - Not stacked; not a standard faceted statistical chart, though the two main panels function like a simple split by tournament.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Tournament division (Women’s / Men’s) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side panel; title text |
| Round | Ordinal | Horizontal position across the bracket; round headers at top |
| Region | Categorical/nominal | Spatial grouping within each bracket; region labels on edges |
| Team name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to bracket positions |
| Seed number | Ordinal | Numeric text preceding team names |
| Team record (wins-losses) | Quantitative | Parenthetical text in first-round team labels |
| Game score / points | Quantitative | Numeric text placed beside teams in each matchup |
| Advancement / winner progression | Categorical/nominal (outcome status) | Connecting bracket lines leading to the next round |
| Champion | Categorical/nominal | Center-most final label/box in each bracket |
